{"id": "7:205/q01", "question": "Who is addressed by “remember your Lord”?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular imperative continues the Prophet’s address or addresses listeners and believers more broadly.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q01/p1", "position": "The Prophet is addressed, with guidance extending to the community or all accountable people.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Mawardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, and Study Quran extend the address generally. Abū Ḥayyān calls the Prophet the apparent addressee and says protection from error makes the community the intended recipients of the final warning. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the community emulates his obligations unless specifically barred. Iṣlāḥī notes the singular can denote a plural audience, comparing 7:199."}, {"id": "7:205/q01/p2", "position": "The Qur’an listener is addressed, including one listening in prayer or at a sermon.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd connects the command to the preceding order to listen (7:204); Ṭabrisī reports listeners raised supplicatory voices upon hearing Paradise or Hell. Ibn Kathīr objects that this would conflict with attentive listening; Ālūsī calls the congregant reading remote."}, {"id": "7:205/q01/p3", "position": "Every person is directly addressed.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports reflection on signs and proofs to know God's attributes; Abū Ḥayyān records it as an alternative."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q02", "question": "What remembrance is commanded?", "turns_on": "Whether the speech wording confines remembrance to prayer or invocation, or encompasses inward reflection and all acts of remembering.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q02/p1", "position": "Recitation in prayer, sometimes specifically a follower’s quiet recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās ties it to prayer and 7:204's account of companions confusing the Prophet by reciting behind him; Qatāda specifies silent recitation behind an imam. Al-Shāfiʿī places a congregant’s recitation after the imam finishes. Jishumī prefers this because the verse specifies speech below loudness; Qatāda’s identification of dawn and afternoon can limit it to those prayers. Wāḥidī extends it across silent and audible prayers, citing 17:110."}, {"id": "7:205/q02/p2", "position": "Inward awareness, reflection on God's signs, blessings, attributes, and commands, joined to obedience.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī requires heeding Qur’anic admonitions and limits; Thaʿlabī adds faith in signs and obedience. Māwardī specifies reflection on favors. Rāzī requires understanding uttered words, comparing a meaningless sale formula. Ālūsī reports that bare tongue recitation may earn no reward; Ghazālī says love and intimacy are required."}, {"id": "7:205/q02/p3", "position": "Every form of remembrance, including Qur’an, supplication, praise, glorification, the testimony of unity, and other invocations.", "reasons": "Zayd b. Aslam lists glorification, unity, and praise; Kashshāf and Nasafī explicitly broaden the scope. Ibn ʿĀshūr lists testimony, ḥawqala, tasbīḥ, takbīr and thanks. Kur’an Yolu distinguishes general dhikr from fixed Sufi formulas and cites 13:28 and 24:37."}, {"id": "7:205/q02/p4", "position": "Supplication to God.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī explicitly calls it quiet supplication; Ibn Jurayj and others require humble, subdued prayer. Qurtubī invokes Naḥḥās and 7:55. Ibn ʿAbbās in Thaʿlabī distinguishes aloud supplication and inward fear."}, {"id": "7:205/q02/p5", "position": "Obedience or memory opposed to forgetting.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists these among alternative interpretations; Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī and Biqāʿī make remembered commands and practice part of remembrance."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q03", "question": "Why does the verse say “your Lord”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q03/p1", "position": "It evokes divine care, nearness, beneficence, and the servant’s lowliness, stirring hope alongside fear.", "reasons": "Rāzī invokes God’s uncountable favors at 14:34 and sees hope foregrounded before awe; he quotes a saying that believers’ fear and hope balance. Abū Ḥayyān says “Lord” honors the servant while fitting humility before a master."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q04", "question": "What is meant by remembering God “within yourself”?", "turns_on": "Whether “within yourself” distinguishes a mental act from quiet tongue speech, or denotes the private setting of remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q04/p1", "position": "Inward remembrance takes place in the heart or inner cognition, distinct from speech.", "reasons": "Mujāhid commands heart remembrance. The theologians infer inward speech; Rāzī rejects reducing it to knowledge, because known concepts cannot be sought anew and absent ones cannot be conceived. Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s tongue only reading: coordination distinguishes inward from verbal remembrance. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes nafs may mean soul, embodied self, cognition, or private self, comparing 5:116."}, {"id": "7:205/q04/p2", "position": "It means quiet verbal remembrance with tongue movement, audible to oneself.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites “below loud speech” as proof; Bursevī says quiet speech protects sincerity. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats dhikr as verbal, including Qur’an and praise. Abū Ḥayyān disputes the inference."}, {"id": "7:205/q04/p3", "position": "It means remembrance in solitude or privately, as well as in company.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the Bukhārī sacred saying contrasting private remembrance with a gathering; Abū Ḥayyān calls a private state unseen by others the noblest."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q05", "question": "Why is inward remembrance urged?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q05/p1", "position": "Concealment protects sincerity, prevents display, aids reflection, and increases receptivity.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Jubbaʾī stress distance from ostentation; Kashshāf, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, and Study Quran say quiet favors reflection. Sulamī’s Ḥusayn warns against publicizing even to oneself for recompense. Rāzī calls inward humility most beneficial. Bursevī links quiet speech to an answered prayer."}, {"id": "7:205/q05/p2", "position": "The servant realizes God sees and is near, and remembrance transforms inner and outer life.", "reasons": "Tustarī calls true dhikr certainty of divine sight, modesty, and choosing God; he glosses the world-curse report as avoiding sin under that awareness. Study Quran says it can lead to presence and unveiling."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q06", "question": "What is promised to one who remembers God privately or publicly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q06/p1", "position": "God reciprocates private remembrance privately and public remembrance in a better, nobler assembly.", "reasons": "Reported from ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr across several collections; Ibn ʿĀshūr names Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī for the sacred report. Ālūsī gives no source or grading."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q07", "question": "What do “humbly and fearfully” require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q07/p1", "position": "The rememberer humbles and submits to God while fearing Him or His punishment.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī compares 6:63; Jishumī cites the idiom “the fever humbled me” and links abasement to unmet duties. Bursevī distinguishes humble entreaty from earnest ibtihāl. Ibn ʿĀshūr says humility can connote raised speech, whereas fear evokes soft speech; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts believers’ worldly humility with unbelievers’ abasement on the promised Day."}, {"id": "7:205/q07/p2", "position": "Humility and awe correspond to spiritual stations and the interplay of divine beauty and majesty.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes beginners’ fear of punishment from knowers’ fear of majesty; unveiled beauty sustains while majesty overwhelms. Qāshānī associates humility with differentiation within unity and fear with the self claiming a share. Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees loving attraction and majestic repulsion; Ālūsī says the degree varies by station. Rāzī reads Wāsiṭī’s “gratitude is shirk” as criticizing the claim that thanks independently repay divine gifts, while humble gratitude shows servitude."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q08", "question": "How are “humbly and fearfully” parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusatives state a manner, the motive of remembrance, or a supplied verbal action.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q08/p1", "position": "They are circumstantial accusatives or verbal nouns functioning adverbially: remember humbly and fearfully.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Qurtubī, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Bursevī give this construction. Ālūsī also allows an omitted noun, “possessing humility and fear,” and rejects a purpose parse."}, {"id": "7:205/q08/p2", "position": "They are purpose complements: remembrance is motivated by humility and fear.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān connects them to hope of reward and fear of punishment; Samīn explicitly prefers this because those motives cause remembrance. Ālūsī objects."}, {"id": "7:205/q08/p3", "position": "They are semantic verbal nouns supplied from an unmentioned verb.", "reasons": "Samīn reports Abū al-Baqāʾ’s root-independent semantic derivation but calls it remote. Ālūsī rejects a verbal noun supplied from an omitted verb."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q09", "question": "What supplication customs accompany the discussion of humble remembrance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q09/p1", "position": "Hands are raised in supplication and wiped over the face afterward.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports ʿUmar’s statement that the Prophet wiped his face after prayer, relates it to the prayer mark in 48:29, and interprets the gesture as returning blessing and uniting outward and inward orientation. Asrār Muḥammadiyya assigns palm positions for requests, distress, and imprecation; Abū Yazīd’s dream favors an uncovered hand. Bursevī compares the petitioner to someone pointing toward a sultan’s treasury and cites provision in heaven at 51:22."}, {"id": "7:205/q09/p2", "position": "Supplication is an earnest bodily devotion sustained by hope of divine generosity.", "reasons": "Bursev

{"id": "7:205/q10", "question": "What does “khīfatan” mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q10/p1", "position": "It means fear; the underlying wāw in khawfah changes to yāʾ after kasra.", "reasons": "Majāz says the wāw drops; Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī and Bursevī describe the vowel-conditioned replacement. Naḥḥās calls khīfah singular and khawf collective of the same sense, with al-Farrāʾ recording khīf. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the noun does not by itself specify a posture. Samarraʾī also allows a manner or inward-state noun by comparison with other paired verbal forms."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q11", "question": "What variant is read for “khīfatan”?", "turns_on": "Whether the word derives from fear or from hiding.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q11/p1", "position": "The common reading is khīfatan, a noun of fear.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls it the common reading; Rāzī and others explain the wāw-to-yāʾ formation."}, {"id": "7:205/q11/p2", "position": "Some read khifyatan or khafiyatan, indicating concealment.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the faʿla pattern from the verb “hide”; Samīn notes reversal of fāʾ and yāʾ. Rāzī distinguishes beginners concealing worship to avoid display from perfected lovers concealing it through protective jealousy, citing a saying that one who knows God has a silent tongue."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q12", "question": "What fear can accompany remembrance?", "turns_on": "The servant's station and the feared object: punishment and outcome, divine majesty, or self-appropriation.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q12/p1", "position": "Fear of punishment, failures in duties, an adverse ending, or the prior decree.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī fears punishment for neglecting admonitions and limits. Rāzī lists deficient works and inability to repay blessings, then prior decree, citing the saying that the pen has dried. Bursevī reports Ibn al-Shaykh on the same fears but restricts fear of ending and decree to ordinary believers rather than prophets or perfected saints."}, {"id": "7:205/q12/p2", "position": "Awe of divine majesty, heightened by knowledge and spiritual realization.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes this from beginners’ fear of punishment; Ṭabāṭabāʾī links it with majestic names; Ālūsī’s poem describes lowering the gaze through reverence."}, {"id": "7:205/q12/p3", "position": "Fear that the self takes credit or claims a share in remembrance.", "reasons": "Qāshānī locates this fear in the self and its pretensions."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q13", "question": "How loud should spoken remembrance be?", "turns_on": "Whether “below loudness” requires audible self-hearing, permits silent inner remembrance, or sets recitation levels for particular prayers.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q13/p1", "position": "Quiet yet audible to oneself, at a moderate volume below shouting.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Rāzī require self-hearing; Rāzī links 17:110 and 19:3. Qurtubī calls loudness prohibited. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the middle volume permits differing levels of energy in speech. Bayḍāwī places it above a whisper. Bursevī says the imam needs only enough volume for the congregation; reports of ʿUmar and Abū Bakr being told to lower and slightly raise their voices set a middle course."}, {"id": "7:205/q13/p2", "position": "In prayer, quiet prayers are read silently and audible prayers low enough to avoid excessive volume.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī invokes 17:110 for the middle course; Baghawī says the imam should remain audible to those behind. Zayd reports both a ban on dawn audibility and a further report allowing it."}, {"id": "7:205/q13/p3", "position": "Keep remembrance wholly inward, with no audible speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd forbids audibility; Mujāhid commands heart remembrance. Ibn Kathīr separates inward remembrance from quiet speech. Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise distinguishes two modes."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q14", "question": "Why avoid loudness, and when may vocal remembrance be raised?", "turns_on": "Whether quiet is an absolute norm or a contextual rule governed by sincerity, disturbance, and devotional benefit.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q14/p1", "position": "Avoid shouting because God is near and hearing, and quiet protects humility, sincerity, and reflection.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, and Biqāʿī cite the Prophet telling loudly supplicating companions that they were not calling one deaf or absent. Study Quran and Ibn Kathīr cite the question about a near or distant Lord answered by 2:186. Abū Ḥayyān compares etiquette before the Prophet in 49:2 and 49:4; Study Quran adds 31:19 and 4:142. Ibn Kathīr says loud recitation provoked polytheists’ insults."}, {"id": "7:205/q14/p2", "position": "Moderate audibility is permitted or useful when it benefits listeners, focuses the reciter, dispels sleep, or helps a beginner.", "reasons": "Nawawī permits it absent display or disturbance; Anwar al-Mashāriq reports agreement on moderate volume. A Kashshāf commentator and Suhrawardī use vocal repetition to interrupt thoughts. Bursevī notes purified practitioners of loud dhikr have arguments. Ibn ʿAjībah rejects banning communal dhikr, citing later public mosque practice in Medina."}, {"id": "7:205/q14/p3", "position": "The verse can be applied to keeping the two testimonies quiet in the call to prayer or to banning loud communal dhikr.", "reasons": "Burhān applies it to the call to prayer. Study Quran reports an attempted prohibition of loud Sufi dhikr, opposed by Ibn ʿAjībah on historical grounds."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q15", "question": "How is “below loud speech” construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordinated phrase is an implied speaking manner, a direct adverbial coordination, or a second state beside inward remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q15/p1", "position": "It modifies an omitted circumstantial expression: remember while speaking below loudness.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī and Ālūsī supply a speaking state; Samīn favors this over treating dūn as an inflected coordinated noun."}, {"id": "7:205/q15/p2", "position": "It coordinates with “within yourself,” adding quiet tongue speech to inward remembrance.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers this because coordination implies difference; Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguish inward and quiet spoken states."}, {"id": "7:205/q15/p3", "position": "It coordinates directly with the circumstantial accusatives, meaning “humbly and moderately.”", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ offers this; Samīn calls it weak because dūn normally stays adverbial. Ālūsī records a version needing no ellipsis."}, {"id": "7:205/q15/p4", "position": "Dūn is a locative adverbial noun governing its genitive complement.", "reasons": "Sībawayh classifies dūn among nouns locating things, contrasting genitive government by particles or ordinary nouns. His related examples discuss case after bāʾ and ʿalā; he rejects treating bifa wqih as an idiom and cites Kaʿb’s “wa-dūna Maʿadd.”"}]}
{"id": "7:205/q16", "question": "What time does “ghudū” denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the time word names a stretch of morning or points to the dawn prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q16/p1", "position": "The morning or early part of the day.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the first half of daylight; Ibn Kathīr says its beginning. Bursevī and Ālūsī narrow it from dawn prayer until sunrise, whereas Biqāʿī includes forenoon."}, {"id": "7:205/q16/p2", "position": "The dawn prayer or its end.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās identify it as Fajr; Mujāhid specifies the end of the dawn prayer. Ibn ʿAbbās invokes 24:36 when asked where dawn prayer appears in scripture."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q17", "question": "How is “ghudū” formed?", "turns_on": "Whether ghudū is a time-designating verbal noun or a plural of ghudwah.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q17/p1", "position": "It is a plural of ghudwah, “mornings.”", "reasons": "Al-Layth compares ghada wāt; Wāḥidī cites a rajaz line using singular ghudwah. Abū Ḥayyān says the plural matches the generic evening plural. Al-Qāmūs supports this analysis."}, {"id": "7:205/q17/p2", "position": "It is a verbal noun of going out in the morning, used for the time; an implied “times of” may balance the evening plural.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Rāzī compare 34:12. Abū Ḥayyān treats the two collective time spans as balanced; Samīn supplies “times of morning.” Ṣiḥāḥ records ghadā, yaghdū, ghudūwan and opposes it to rawāḥ. Biqāʿī calls it singular on this account."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q18", "question": "Do morning and evening limit when remembrance is required?", "turns_on": "Whether the endpoints name a permanent daily practice, particular prayers, or exemplify continuous remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q18/p1", "position": "They stand for all times, calling for continuous remembrance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says every day and both ends; Rāzī cites Ibn ʿAbbās on 3:191 that another human posture would likewise have been named. Biqāʿī says the two endpoints represent day and night. Study Quran cites many morning-evening passages; Iṣlāḥī compares remembrance to breath sustaining the soul."}, {"id": "7:205/q18/p2", "position": "They are especially meritorious or receptive periods for remembrance.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Study Quran stress their merit. Ṭabrisī and Ālūsī say the heart is then freer from livelihood. Rāzī, Bursevī, and Study Quran point to waking and sleep, light and darkness, death and resurrection as signs of divine power. Ālūsī also reports angels changing shifts then."}, {"id": "7:205/q18/p3", "position": "They refer to specified prayers or to the older practice of two daily prayers before five became obligatory.", "reasons": "Qatāda identifies Fajr and ʿAṣr; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān report a pre-five-prayers setting.

Ibn Kathīr calls the verse Meccan and earlier than the Night Journey; Wāḥidī’s all-prayers account differs from Qatāda’s two-prayer limit."}, {"id": "7:205/q18/p4", "position": "They cover the normal daylight span, with night generally reserved for sleep yet still subject to the ban on heedlessness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr divides daylight into morning and evening, cites 73:2 for waking devotion at night, and says the closing ban extends beyond daylight."}]}

{"id": "7:205/q20", "question": "What time does “āṣāl” denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the evening word begins after the afternoon prayer or already spans noon to afternoon.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q20/p1", "position": "Evening or late afternoon, commonly from the afternoon prayer until sunset.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites poetry with aṣāʾil; Majāz cites Abū Dhuʾayb, and Wāḥidī cites al-Nābigha. Abū Wāʾil’s use of āṣalnā at sunset attests ordinary usage. Jawharī gives further plurals with poetry. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the latter half of daylight until sunset."}, {"id": "7:205/q20/p2", "position": "The period between noon and afternoon.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣakhr supplies this narrower, earlier interval; Durr repeats his report."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q21", "question": "How is “āṣāl” formed and why is late afternoon called aṣīl?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural passes through aṣl, forms directly from aṣīl, or begins from singular aṣl; the etymological explanations connect day's end to a beginning or base.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q21/p1", "position": "Āṣāl is a plural of aṣl, itself a plural of aṣīl.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Farrāʾ describe a plural of a plural. Samīn and Ālūsī say direct aṣīl to āṣāl is morphologically disfavored because faʿīl does not normally take afʿāl. Al-Farrāʾ also glosses muʾṣilīn as entering evening. Samīn records a poem with the diminutive aṣīlāl and Kufan and Basran analyses."}, {"id": "7:205/q21/p2", "position": "Āṣāl is a direct plural of aṣīl.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Ibn Kathīr, and others compare yamīn and aymān. Samīn explicitly opposes the claimed morphological bar."}, {"id": "7:205/q21/p3", "position": "The name aṣīl is tied to aṣl, a beginning or base, because day’s end meets night’s beginning.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī sees the day descending toward its bottom; Jishumī calls it the point where day ends and night begins. Rāzī and Biqāʿī link it to the coming night’s beginning."}, {"id": "7:205/q21/p4", "position": "Āṣāl is a plural of aṣl treated as a singular evening noun.", "reasons": "Samīn says this avoids a plural-of-plural account and notes aṣlān. Al-Farrāʾ reportedly allows aṣul as singular; Ālūsī compares ʿunuq."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q22", "question": "What variant is read for “āṣāl”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q22/p1", "position": "Abū Mujliz reads wa-l-īṣāl, a verbal noun meaning entry into evening.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, and Ālūsī attribute the reading to Abū Mujliz; Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī also report it. The verbal noun parallels ghudū when the latter is parsed as a verbal noun."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q23", "question": "Who are “the heedless,” and what is forbidden?", "turns_on": "Whether heedlessness is failure of dhikr, wider disobedience, failure in specific duties, or loss of inward witnessing.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q23/p1", "position": "Those who neglect remembrance, recitation, reflection, or the commanded supplication.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Wāḥidī Wajīz specify neglecting prayer recitation; Ṭabarī means ignoring Quranic lessons and divine limits. Tustarī says even one breath without dhikr is heedlessness, repeated by Sulamī; Abū Ḥayyān likewise urges no lapse. Bursevī says the heart must attend to God’s majesty behind the tongue’s words. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows differing human needs and duties, while Ṭabāṭabāʾī says occasional lapse should be remedied lest heedlessness settle."}, {"id": "7:205/q23/p2", "position": "Those who neglect obedience to God's commands and prohibitions more broadly.", "reasons": "Māwardī attributes this to the majority; Tustarī says heedlessness among the elite is settling into a thing, among ordinary people pride in it. Sulamī says heedlessness includes failure to grasp realities."}, {"id": "7:205/q23/p3", "position": "Heedlessness can appear as failure to know Friday, neglect of morning devotion, or neglect of one's religious self.", "reasons": "Bukayr b. al-Akhnas says arriving at Friday without recognizing it counts. Durr reports a Prophetic threefold list: neglecting God’s remembrance, dawn-to-sunrise, and neglect of one’s religious self. Mālik’s ungraded ʿUmar letter applies the warning to observing prayer times."}, {"id": "7:205/q23/p4", "position": "On the inward reading, heedlessness is forgetting essential unity or treating oneself as the true rememberer.", "reasons": "Qāshānī urges vigilance when self traits dominate; Ibn Ḥusayn says only God truly remembers God. Ālūsī and spiritual masters distinguish levels of witnessing and vigilance."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q24", "question": "Why say “do not be among the heedless”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q24/p1", "position": "It reinforces the command and warns against joining a settled class marked by heedlessness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the group expression is stronger and clearer than simply “do not be heedless.” Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes rooted heedlessness from a momentary lapse; Abū Ḥayyān calls the ban reinforcement."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q25", "question": "What practices and reports are linked to remembrance amid heedlessness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q25/p1", "position": "A person remembering God among the heedless is likened to a fighter defending the two groups.", "reasons": "Durr transmits this Prophetic comparison."}, {"id": "7:205/q25/p2", "position": "Regular devotional practice keeps the soul turned to God and should be maintained for God's right.", "reasons": "Ibn Malik says habit shapes the soul; Bursevī warns not to abandon litanies for extraordinary gifts. A knower says litany’s reward ends with the worldly practice; Bursevī cites a report that mercy grants Paradise and deeds distribute its rewards, and Hafiz’s verse prefers divine intimacy to houris."}, {"id": "7:205/q25/p3", "position": "Remembrance has rewards and divine companionship beyond the garden's ordinary rewards.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports a saying that remembrance exceeds battlefield encounter and a sacred saying, “I am the companion of whoever remembers Me”; the promised intimacy and witnessing exceed Paradise as usually sought."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q26", "question": "How does the verse connect to the preceding and following discourse?", "turns_on": "The discourse can be read as shifting from public recitation to personal devotion, continuing the listening instruction, or closing the sūra's devotional arc.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q26/p1", "position": "After the order to listen to the Qur’an, it tells the Prophet or listener how to remember and supplicate.", "reasons": "Jishumī ties it to 7:204, while Abū Muslim links it to 7:196, “My protector is God,” as a command to tell them to remember. Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguish the Prophet’s loud recitation for others from his own inward devotion. Ālūsī suggests واذكر may coordinate with قل or begin fresh address; Ibn Kathīr rejects making it an act performed while listening."}, {"id": "7:205/q26/p2", "position": "Morning and evening remembrance parallels other commands to glorify God and reflects a contrast between worldly humility and final abasement.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites 50:39; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts believers’ pious humility now with unbelievers’ fearful abasement on the promised Day. Iṣlāḥī reads the counsel as help for the Prophet to withstand baseless objections."}, {"id": "7:205/q26/p3", "position": "The closing remembrance passage prepares the angels' example and the next sūra's portrait of believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says angels' exertion after the heedlessness warning encourages earnest obedience. Ālūsī links al-Aʿrāf’s guidance, mercy, listening, and remembrance with al-Anfāl’s believers whose faith increases on hearing verses."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q27", "question": "What inward stages of remembrance are drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "The notes map the command to awareness, progressive practice, mutual soul-body effects, and symbolic time.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q27/p1", "position": "True dhikr is sustained awareness of God’s sight, nearness, and unity, reshaping conduct.", "reasons": "Tustarī defines it as certainty God sees and one chooses Him over self; Sulamī says hidden remembrance is finest. Qāshānī reads God as present within and cites 33:21; Ālūsī connects following the Prophet with divine qualities. Study Quran associates dhikr with unveiling and presence."}, {"id": "7:205/q27/p2", "position": "Spoken remembrance can awaken imagination and soul; bodily and inward actions strengthen one another.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites sourness

making teeth ache and repeated action forming a disposition; he traces words through imagination to spirit and back. {"id": "7:205/q28", "question": "What supporting grammatical and rhetorical examples accompany discussion of the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q28/p1", "position": "Poetic similes show how a later detail can delimit an earlier image precisely.", "reasons": "Jurjānī’s startled crow example conveys swift flight driven by fear or release; his hawk-beak comparison selects only the curved upper stroke of a left-handed jīm, clarified by later letters and a mention of thought."}, {"id": "7:205/q28/p2", "position": "Verbal and nominal predicates differ in aspect and information structure.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says finite verbs present repeated unfolding, participles a settled trait; 35:3’s yarzuqukum would change sense as rāziq lakum. “Zayd is departing” and “Zayd is the departing one” serve different listener knowledge, despite comparable predicate slots."}]}
{"id": "7:205/q29", "question": "What practical issues are raised about counting verses?", "turns_on": "Whether knowing exact verse boundaries has legal and recitational consequences.", "positions": [{"id": "7:205/q29/p1", "position": "Verse counts and endings matter for prayer, sermons, night recitation, stopping, and inimitability.", "reasons": "Itqān cites a sound report of sixty to one hundred verses at dawn prayer and reports reward thresholds from ten through one thousand night verses. It calls a full verse necessary for sermons, though a disputed ending is unresolved. Hudhalī says a half-verse is insufficient by consensus for prayer and that inimitability requires a full verse."}, {"id": "7:205/q29/p2", "position": "Verse counting is dismissed as lacking substantive knowledge.", "reasons": "Zaʿfarānī alleges commercial motives; Hudhalī rejects the dismissal because endings govern stopping and legal minimums."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q01", "question": "Who is addressed as believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q01/p1", "position": "Those who already profess and affirm faith.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi say this is undisputed; Biqa'i distinguishes profession by the tongue, and Qashani describes belief in the unseen."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q02", "question": "Why repeat the address by faith?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q02/p1", "position": "It stirs professing believers to make their faith real through wholehearted obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says naming faith reminds them what impels obedience; Biqa'i says they must respond eagerly."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q03", "question": "What does responding to God and the Messenger mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the derived form adds a request for response or is synonymous with ajāba.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q03/p1", "position": "Answer, obey, and comply with God's and the Messenger's summons.", "reasons": "Majaz cites Ka'b ibn Sa'd's poem and both direct and lām constructions; Zajjaj and Jishumi cite a poet's lam yastajibhu; Ibn Atiyya notes istajāba normally takes lām while ajāba usually does not. Ibn Abbas glosses it as obedience, and Biqa'i applies this to every call."}, {"id": "8:24/q03/p2", "position": "It can mean seeking an answer.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this alternate morphology, while the cited poetic use favors simply answering."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q04", "question": "How broad is the command to respond?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition narrows the calls covered, and how the prayer incident bears on the command.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q04/p1", "position": "Every valid call of the Messenger calls for obedience, including an immediate summons.", "reasons": "Mawardi links response wording to the summons. Ibn Jawzi transmits Ibn Abbas's 'everything'; Razi argues the imperative and subsequent threat make it obligatory, with Ubayy's rebuke as practical report evidence. Biqa'i says the condition does not restrict the command; Ibn Ashur treats 'what gives life' as explanatory and cites the prayer incident. Kuran Yolu extends following the Prophet after his death to Quran and Sunna."}, {"id": "8:24/q04/p2", "position": "The verse primarily commands obedience to guidance, while the Prophet also applied it to a literal call.", "reasons": "Tabari says Ubay's prayer incident does not confine the verse to prayer, and Ibn Ashur cites 3:172 and 3:104 for broader guidance."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q05", "question": "Who was praying when the Prophet called and cited this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrated worshipper is Ubayy, Abu Saʿid, or Hudhayfa, and whether these are separate similar incidents.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q05/p1", "position": "Ubayy ibn Kaʿb delayed his answer during prayer; the Prophet cited the verse.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra gives versions in which Ubayy turns or hastens but waits to finish, then promises to answer promptly even in prayer. In continuations the Prophet teaches him al-Fatiha as the unparalleled seven oft-repeated verses; Biqa'i notes Tirmidhi's hasan sahih grading. Ibn Ashur says Ibn Atiyya's Malik version is the same report as Tirmidhi's."}, {"id": "8:24/q05/p2", "position": "Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla finished his prayer before answering; the Prophet cited the verse.", "reasons": "Bukhari's version adds that the Prophet taught him al-Fatiha as the greatest sura and seven oft-repeated. Ibn Atiyya cites Bukhari and Muslim as naming him rather than Ubayy; Ibn Ashur and others preserve both similar incidents."}, {"id": "8:24/q05/p3", "position": "A similar incident is reported with Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman at the Battle of the Trench.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports it; Ibn Ashur says multiple cases underline the special force of the Messenger's call."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q06", "question": "What does the prayer incident imply for interrupting prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the call is a Prophetic privilege, a necessary interruption, or an act within prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q06/p1", "position": "An urgent summons permits interrupting prayer, including comparable danger to others.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi and Alusi give an urgent-matter reading; Alusi says Ubayy's report alone does not establish that prayer remained intact. Awza'i's child-at-the-well case exemplifies necessity."}, {"id": "8:24/q06/p2", "position": "Answering the Prophet is required and need not invalidate prayer.", "reasons": "Shafi'i says a required utterance or act in prayer does not invalidate it because answering him is itself obedience. Baydawi says the apparent hadith favors this. Qurtubi and Kuran Yolu extend the logic to Awza'i's example of warning a child near a well."}, {"id": "8:24/q06/p3", "position": "This duty to answer during prayer is specific to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Kashshaf reports the privilege view; Biqa'i insists the Prophet's distinct authority and discusses when an act is exclusive, citing 33:50."}, {"id": "8:24/q06/p4", "position": "Answering is not obligatory and does invalidate prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ruyani's transmitted view, reported by Alusi."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q07", "question": "What wider model of prophetic obedience is drawn from the command?", "turns_on": "How the immediate summons extends to prophetic conduct, precedent, and later followers.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet's calls and acts should be followed as sources of rulings and divine love.", "reasons": "Biqa'i says his protected conveyance makes his acts indicators of rulings; Abu Bakr and Ibn Umar imitated even mount turns, dye and sandals; the Yemen consecration, harvest command, pollination case and jihad/debt distinction illustrate following him. He cites 3:31 for divine love and 33:50 for explicit exclusivity."}, {"id": "8:24/q07/p2", "position": "Following him after his death means following the Quran and Sunna in life.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu distinguishes attending the Prophet in his lifetime from obeying his transmitted guidance later."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q08", "question": "Why is the caller singular after naming God and the Messenger?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q08/p1", "position": "God's call comes through the Messenger, so the two named authorities issue one call.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says naming both reinforces obedience; Baydawi points to the single caller just mentioned; Nasafi compares the preceding verse; Elmalili says the Messenger's call is not distinct from God's."}]}

llows this attachment, and Tabataba'i calls it common usage."}, {"id": "8:24/q09/p2", "position": "The lām attaches to 'calls,' whose construction takes a lām.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan distinguishes the two prepositions' functions and cites poetry; Qurtubi says limā yuḥyīkum attaches to the response, giving the alternative parse."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q10", "question": "Why say lām rather than ilā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q10/p1", "position": "It conveys the nearness of obedience's benefit.", "reasons": "Biqa'i links the choice to life through faith and knowledge rather than the heedlessness of 8:22."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q11", "question": "What is the life-giving call?", "turns_on": "Which life is meant: faith, revelation, battle, martyrdom, knowledge, worldly welfare, or lasting life; and whether the wording restricts the answer.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q11/p1", "position": "Jihad or battle restores the community's strength, protects its life, and leads to reward.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Ibn Ishaq recall honor after humiliation and strength after weakness; Wahidi/Farra say abandonment emboldens enemies; Kashshaf cites 2:179, and Razi adds martyrdom and 29:64. Ibn Qutayba says jihad revives religion."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p2", "position": "Every truth or act of obedience that brings good life in this world and the next.", "reasons": "Tabari includes jihad, Quranic judgment, worldly good repute, and eternal Gardens, rejecting restriction to initial Islam because believers are addressed. Razi says every divine command carries reward; Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, and Tabataba'i prefer breadth. Ibn Ashur names sound belief, character, social reform, courage, freedom, and livelihood; Tabataba'i includes life near God. Bukhari glosses it as what sets people right; Kuran Yolu links Islam's peace and security to law and justice without oppression."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p3", "position": "The Quran and its commands revive and protect people.", "reasons": "Qatada says it brings life, chastity or confidence, rescue and protection in both abodes. Wahidi adds knowledge and useful practice; Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi stress commands and prohibitions and their eternal reward."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p4", "position": "Martyrdom gives life with God.", "reasons": "Al-Qutaybi and others cite 3:169; jihad can be its means. Some reports present martyrdom as its own answer, and Wahidi combines honor, martyrs' life, and Paradise."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p5", "position": "The truth itself is the call, with faith among its meanings.", "reasons": "Mujahid repeatedly gives 'truth'; Wahidi says this can encompass Quran, faith, and jihad. Ibn Jawzi records both truth and faith from him."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p6", "position": "Faith or Islam revives hearts from the death of disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi gives the recurrent account; Wahidi cites 6:95, Razi 30:19. Qurtubi describes monotheism as heart-life. Tabari and Ibn Atiyya object that the audience already believes, while Tabataba'i allows it as an application."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p7", "position": "Religious knowledge and sound action are life; ignorance is death.", "reasons": "Zajjaj calls knowledge life's cause. Kashshaf, Baydawi, and Nasafi cite the poem that dresses the ignorant dead man in a shroud. Ibn Ashur explains figurative life as fulfillment of a thing's purpose, citing plant growth and 6:122. Tabataba'i joins knowledge to innate guidance."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p8", "position": "Paradise or enduring afterlife bliss is the promised life.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq distinguish lasting bliss from its means; Abu Ali al-Jurjani and Razi cite 29:64. Tabataba'i explains a higher life of faith, spirit, and righteous company with 50:22, 58:22, 6:122, 2:253, 42:52, and 16:97."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p9", "position": "The call revives worldly affairs, honor, and livelihood.", "reasons": "Farra says it revives affairs; Ibn Jawzi lists reform of worldly and otherworldly affairs, good repute, and spoils; Abu Hayyan also records bodily life. Kuran Yolu says guidance contributes to health, psychological strength, and purposeful living."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p10", "position": "It gives inward life through purification, tawḥīd, and nearness to God.", "reasons": "Junayd describes struggle and lasting life through the Real; Ja'far connects obedience, true life and gnosis to 16:97. Qushayri describes light of unity after effacement. Qashani differentiates inner purification and faith-realization; Sulami distinguishes soul, heart, and self. Burhan's landscape image of Qur'anic sections portrays the seeker journeying away from all else toward vision."}, {"id": "8:24/q11/p11", "position": "It summons believers to ʿAli's walāya.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq is cited through Abu al-Rabi and al-Baqir through Ibn Mardawayh and Abu al-Jarud; Tabataba'i classifies these as applications of the general verse."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q12", "question": "How does the verse use 'life'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'life' denotes spiritual fulfillment, bodily preservation, or everlasting afterlife.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q12/p1", "position": "Life is metaphorical for the knowledge, faith, and fulfilled human purpose that animate an otherwise dead heart.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur distinguishes bodily life, which supports perception and movement, from analogical life that completes purpose; he also notes preservation of literal life in 2:179 and 5:32. Al-Alusi calls the causal naming metaphor or metonymy. Tabataba'i makes true life subtler than bodily awareness."}, {"id": "8:24/q12/p2", "position": "Life is the enduring reality of the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i contrasts 29:64 with worldly play and describes faith's light and the Holy Spirit as degrees of life."}, {"id": "8:24/q12/p3", "position": "Life includes bodily survival, health, and worldly well-being.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares retribution and saving a life; Kuran Yolu emphasizes religious practice, health, social safety, and psychological resilience."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q13", "question": "What is the inflection of yuḥyīkum?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q13/p1", "position": "The final yāʾ bears an unpronounced nominative ḍamma because it is heavy; assimilation is impermissible.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi give the same grammatical account."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q14", "question": "What does ḥawl mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q14/p1", "position": "It means to intervene, separate, or change a state.", "reasons": "Raghib, cited by Alusi, gives change and separation; Tabari says interposing between two things is placing a barrier; Tabataba'i defines ḥaylūla as interposition."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q15", "question": "What does 'heart' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether 'heart' names the cognitive faculty or what it holds.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q15/p1", "position": "The inward faculty of cognition, reason, feeling, and intention.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Qurtubi cite 50:37 for heart as intellect; Razi says loss of intellect ends legal responsibility. Tabataba'i says qalb names the organ and, in Quranic use, the soul acting through inner faculties; Kuran Yolu includes consciousness, reason, and feelings."}, {"id": "8:24/q15/p2", "position": "The heart's contents, including hopes and desires.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari lists wishes for survival, victory, conquest; Qadarites gloss the intended content of heart. Asad cites Raghib on the gap between desire and action."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q16", "question": "How does God come between a person and the heart?", "turns_on": "Whether interposition describes sovereign control, specific moral prevention, lost capacity, nearness and knowledge, mortality, changed emotions, or spiritual veiling.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q16/p1", "position": "God owns and governs hearts, turning beliefs, intentions, perception, and emotions at will.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers the unrestricted wording: a barrier may withhold faith, unbelief, perception or understanding, and no report excludes the others. Razi argues causes of knowledge and motives cannot regress through human intentions; Tabataba'i grounds sovereignty in God's ownership of every created faculty, citing 13:41, 64:1, 50:16, 40:16 and 82:19. Al-Alusi calls the phrase representative metaphor; Biqa'i a metonym of complete power."}, {"id": "8:24/q16/p2", "position": "God is nearer to the heart than its owner and knows every hidden thought.", "reasons": "Ma'mar, Qatada and many others cite 50:16; Mawdardi and Wahidi say even secrets cannot be concealed. Al-Sadiq's reported account says an act desired by the senses can be rejected inwardly."}, {"id": "8:24/q16/p5", "position": "God can take reason or comprehension from a person.", "reasons": "Mujahid says one then cannot know what one is doing; Ibn al-Anbari and Abu Bakr urge action while rational. ever access to the heart; obey before the chance ends.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Isa, al-Jubba'i and others urge repentance, sincere purification, and action before death, loss of reason or another affliction. {"id": "8:24/q17", "question": "What does the interposition imply about human choice and divine justice?", "turns_on": "Whether divine governance creates inner states directly, how capacity makes command meaningful, and what follows for responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q17/p1", "position": "God creates beliefs, motives, and all acquired acts; hearts remain under His will.", "reasons": "Razi argues that independently acquiring knowledge presupposes knowledge and human creation of a motive yields an infinite regress. {"id": "8:24/q18", "question": "What practical warning follows from God coming between a person and the heart?", "turns_on": "Which power of God is emphasized: loss of time and capacity, knowledge of the inward state, or the ability to change fear.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q18/p1", "position": "Respond promptly while faith, understanding, sincerity, and opportunity remain.", "reasons": "Tabari urges fear and obedience lest anger and punishment come.
